source: Melnikoff & Bargh (2018) The mythical number two (Trends in Cognitive Sciences, opinion paper)
finding: Attacks the typology, not any one theory. The claim is that the features of Type 1 (unintentional, uncontrollable, unconscious, efficient) and Type 2 (the opposites) are assumed to line up, but nobody has measured how well they line up. With four binary feature sets there are 16 combinations and the typology says only 2 are common. They list mixed cases (skilled typing is intentional but unconscious; language production; problem solving that is unconscious but inefficient). They add that Type 2 is not 'good' and Type 1 not 'bad': conscious deliberation can give worse choices and rationalisation. Advice: study each feature one by one, assume no correlation until measured.
numbers: No data of their own. Counts: 16 cells vs 2 predicted. No correlation between features is reported by anyone, per the authors. A rebuttal by Pennycook and colleagues (same journal, 2018) says the target is a straw man because a single defining feature is enough; that rebuttal was seen only as a search summary, not opened.
quote: the dual-process typology is a convenient and seductive myth, and we think cognitive science can do better.
limits: Opinion piece. It does not say a speed or task-feature gate fails; it says the two-bin label should not carry assumptions. Evans and Stanovich 2013 had already dropped 'perfectly aligned'.
agent_relevance: Do not let one label (fast, or System 1) stand in for several properties. Our gate should be keyed on separately observable cues (has a computation, has a candidate to test, is a known family), and each cue judged on its own record. This matches the design in K01.

source: Keren & Schul (2009) Two is not always better than one: a critical evaluation of two-system theories (Perspectives on Psychological Science 4(6), 533-550)
finding: A methods critique. Three tests are needed to show two systems: the features must be dichotomous (not continuous), must line up (alignment), and the systems must be separable (double dissociation, system-task match). They go through paradigms (belief bias, conflict, speed manipulations) and say none passes. Belief bias can be explained inside one system that judges validity by logic or by believability. They say two-system models may not be testable with current methods. Alternatives they offer: a many-parts model where parts combine by task demand and goals, or a unimodel where depth of processing varies continuously with task relevance (Kruglanski).
numbers: 18 pages, no new experiment. Argues from published results. No effect sizes.
quote: the theoretical structure of two-system theories is ill-defined
limits: Conceptual. Evans & Stanovich 2013 (a01-a04, d03) reply that the features are correlates, not defining. The unimodel prediction (processing depth varies continuously with perceived task relevance) is not tested against a gate here.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where the mode is set per task by what the task demands (goals, relevance), with depth as a dial, not a fixed switch between two engines. For us: gate on task features and allow several depths (direct, one check, full steps), which a two-bin switch cannot express. No empirical test says this beats a binary gate.

source: Evans & Stanovich (2013) Dual-process theories of higher cognition: advancing the debate (reply to critics; re-read for defining versus correlated features)
finding: Reply to Osman, Keren & Schul, Gigerenzer, Kruglanski. They concede the long feature lists are correlates, not defining. Defining features: Type 1 does not use working memory and is autonomous; Type 2 needs working memory and does cognitive decoupling (holding a hypothetical apart from belief). Speed, capacity, consciousness, normative answers are 'typical correlates'. They accept that individual differences lie on a continuum but hold that the two types are still distinct kinds of process.
numbers: Table of defining features vs typical correlates (about 10 correlates on each side). No new data.
limits: Position paper. The defining-feature move makes the theory harder to refute with a single misaligned correlate, which is the point Melnikoff & Bargh press (d01).
agent_relevance: Gives the function-based definition used in K01: Type 2 is a pass that holds a hypothetical apart, so gate by whether the item needs a candidate held and tested, not by length or speed.

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs agree, are they right? Auditing self-consistency and cross-model agreement as confidence signals (arXiv 2607.08065v2)
finding: Self-agreement across the model's own samples is a positive but weak predictor that the majority answer is right, and it is worse for the most consistent frontier model. Setup: 53 runners, K=50 samples per case at temperature 1.0, 265,000 samples, GPQA Diamond and AIME, gpt-4.1 family (nano, mini, 4.1). Majority-correct vs agreement: Spearman 0.20 to 0.59, all 12 cells positive after Holm correction. gpt-4.1 reaches agreement of 0.8 or more on 77% of GPQA entries and is wrong on 48% of those (95% CI .40 to .56); its correlation is lower than mini's (-0.18 [-0.31,-0.03] GPQA; -0.26 [-0.40,-0.12] AIME). Chain-of-thought only slightly improves the agreement signal. A confidence-routed cascade was dominated by always using the mid-tier model. Option-shuffle control: part of GPQA confidence is positional. An exploratory check on three Claude tiers (haiku-4.5, sonnet-4.6, opus-4.7) shows the same confident-wrong pattern.
numbers: Brier 0.42 and ECE 0.41 for gpt-4.1 on GPQA vs 0.26 and 0.22 for mini with chain-of-thought.
quote: Self-consistency is thus a conditional proxy for correctness, not a standalone confidence score.
limits: Data came from a class assignment (runners could share code; not preregistered; endpoints chosen after earlier analyses; model snapshots not logged). Hard multiple-choice exam questions and competition math, not perturbed-trap items, and not the 3-sample setting we plan. The Claude check is labelled exploratory and agent-mediated.
agent_relevance: Bad news for gap 1 on a modern frontier model: agreement across samples cannot be trusted alone as the signal that my first answer is wrong. A trap item is the case where all samples share the lure, so agreement will be high and wrong. Pair it with outside checks (perturbation, code) and a per-class pass rate, and log it so the rule can be dropped if it does not beat the class base rate.

source: Lyu, Shridhar, Malaviya, Zhang, Elazar, Tandon, Apidianaki, Sachan & Callison-Burch (2025) Calibrating large language models with sample consistency (AAAI 2025)
finding: Confidence taken from the spread of several sampled answers (agreement, entropy of the answer distribution, first-second-distance) predicts correctness better than the model's own stated confidence. Brier score (lower is better), averaged over 9 reasoning datasets and 5 prompt styles: GPT-4 entropy .116, agreement .119, first-second-distance .114, vs verbalised words .154 and verbalised percent .181; GPT-3.5-turbo .205/.221/.207 vs .271/.273. Brier saturates after 15 to 20 samples; 3 to 5 samples already give much better confidence than one sample. Instruction-tuned models are harder to calibrate. In a GSM8K case study the consistency metrics more than doubled macro-F1 for picking out wrong predictions compared with verbalised baselines.
numbers: Eleven models, nine datasets (math word problems, multi-hop QA, planning, relation reasoning). Numbers above are for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-turbo.
limits: Older models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Codex, Llama, Mistral, Olmo). Standard benchmark items, not perturbed traps. No comparison with a plain class pass rate or a constant rule. Older than Ding 2026 (d04), which finds the signal weak on gpt-4.1.
agent_relevance: Supports using sample disagreement over a spoken I-am-not-sure as the S0/S6 trigger (the stated version is the worse signal here). Three to five short samples are enough to read. The gate question stays open: is it better than the class base rate on perturbed items?

source: Boissin, Caparos, Raoelison & De Neys (2021) From bias to sound intuiting: boosting correct intuitive reasoning (Cognition 211, 104645; HAL preprint)
finding: Two-response bat-and-ball (first answer under a deadline of 8 s with memory load, then a free final answer). A short explanation of the bat-and-ball logic (under five minutes) raised correct FIRST responses, not just final ones. Study 1 (N=99, 84 analysed) and Study 2 (N=99, 90 analysed). Initial accuracy gain with training: +30.0 points (Study 1), +45.7 (Study 2); control +11.9 and +6.1. Final accuracy gain: +34.4 and +47.2 (control +9.4, +5.7). Direction of change after training: '11' (correct both times) 41.4% and 52.0%; '01' (fixed on reflection) 7.8% and 9.9%; '00' 50.0% and 36.3%. Before training in the control group '11' was 10.1% and 5.0%, '01' 7.9% and 1.4%, '00' 81.3% and 93.6%. Study 3 retested after at least two months: the effect lasted. Transfer: bat-and-two-balls problems (same logic) improved; basic algebra word problems and other CRT-like lure items did NOT improve. Pre-test: 21.2% correct before explanation, 68.3% on a second free-time problem after.
numbers: Share of final-correct answers that were already correct at the first response: control Study 1 about 56% (10.1/(10.1+7.9)), Study 2 about 78% (5.0/6.4); trained Study 1 about 84%, Study 2 about 84%. Participants from Prolific, native English speakers; those who knew the problem and answered right were excluded.
quote: After training, most participants solved the problems correctly from the outset
limits: Humans, one problem family. Explicit finding: no transfer to untrained problem types. The first response is time-limited and load-limited, which is a proxy for intuition.
agent_relevance: For gap 9: a verified worked example of the family can make the first pass right on near-isomorphic items and does not carry to other families. So worked examples belong in the family's memory entry, keyed to the family; do not expect them to fix unrelated traps. Also supports learning the direct route per family (gap 5).

source: Buric & Konradova (2021) Mindware instantiation as a predictor of logical intuitions in the Cognitive Reflection Test (Studia Psychologica 63(2), 114-128)
finding: Two-response CRT, 908 participants. Initial (time-limited, load) response on conflict items: 37.66% correct, 51.15% the lure, 11.10% other wrong. Final response: 49.25% correct, 46.70% lure, 4% other wrong. Direction of change on conflict items: '11' 28.35%, '00' 36.97%, '01' 25.33%, '10' 9.33%. So of final-correct conflict answers, 28.35/(28.35+25.33), about 53%, were already correct at the first response; the authors say 'more than half'. No-conflict items: 74.79% '11', 20.39% '01'. Mindware instantiation, conflict detection and related variables explained about 10% of the variance in intuitive accuracy. Participants with a technical field of study were 25.3% here vs 14.7% in an earlier sample, offered as one reason for more '01' corrections.
numbers: Fast-correct share of final-correct answers is about 53% on CRT conflict items in this sample.
quote: in more than half of the cases when the response was correct in the final response stage, it was already correct
limits: Sample varies by maths training. Time limit and load imperfectly stop deliberation. This is not the Bago & De Neys 2017 paper itself (not opened here; its 75% to 88% stays unverified).
agent_relevance: For gap 5: the real fast-correct share on the CRT is about half, and it moves with the sample's maths training, so it is a property of the person (or model) and the family, not a constant. Do not trust a direct route in general; keep it as a per-family record fed by outside feedback.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2022 preprint, arXiv 2212.05206v2) Thinking fast and slow in large language models; few-shot studies read again for scope
finding: Study 3: GPT-3-davinci-003 prefixed with 0 to 49 solved CRT-type tasks of the SAME type. Accuracy rose from 2% to 92% after 2 examples (CRT type 2, repeat the stated duration), from 12% to 92% after 7 (type 3), and from 0% to about 78% after 30 (type 1). In Study 5 for semantic illusions, accuracy rose from 18% at 0 examples to over 64% at 10 or more. Unprimed, the model gave the lure in 80% of CRT tasks and 72% of semantic illusions (humans: 55% and 64%). ChatGPT-3.5 was 59% correct and ChatGPT-4 96% on the bespoke items.
numbers: 50 bespoke versions per task type, 200 items in total. Accuracy changes tested with chi-square (p < .001).
limits: The examples came from the same task type as the test items, and these types are template-like, so the gain may be pattern copying, not principle learning. No held-out principle change was tested. Old base model. The later arXiv version was withdrawn and the work was published as a revised paper (Nature Computational Science 2023), so figures here are from this preprint.
agent_relevance: For gap 9: the 2% to 92% jump shows same-family examples fix the first pass fast. It does not show transfer to a changed principle. Ma 2025 (d20) shows principle changes bring the lure back. Treat a worked example as a family-bound prime and test it on held-out principle variants before relying on it.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too) (arXiv 2311.11829); re-read for setup and ablations
finding: S2A has the same model first rewrite the context to drop irrelevant or opinionated parts, then answer from the rewrite only. Model: LLaMA-2-70B-chat for both steps, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.9. TriviaQA with opinions (200 prompts, GPT-4 as judge): baseline 62.8%, oracle (no opinion) 82.0%, S2A 80.3%; instructed prompting ('ignore opinions') 71.7%; S2A that keeps the original text beside the rewrite 74.5%; adding 'think step by step' made things worse. In the suggest-incorrect case instructed prompting scored 38% vs oracle 82%. GSM-IC (100 problems, 3 seeds): in-topic distractor baseline 51.7% to S2A 61.3%; gain about 12 points with random distractors and about 10 with in-topic ones. Long-form arguments: objectivity 3.82 for S2A vs 2.23 baseline vs 3.0 oracle.
numbers: See finding. Small sets (200 and 100 problems).
quote: S2A increases factuality from 62.8% to 80.3% compared to LLaMA-2-70B-chat
limits: One model (LLaMA-2-70B-chat), one lab, GPT-4 judge. The rewrite is a separate call by the same model, so a different pass than the solver is satisfied, but a different model or a code filter as the cleaner was not tested. I searched for replications on current models and found none; a 2026 thesis only describes S2A. Keeping the original text beside the rewrite lost 5.8 points, so the solver must not see the original.
agent_relevance: For gap 6: the 62.8 to 80.3 result is real in the paper but unreplicated in what I could find. Design hint: S1 hands the solver only the cleaned text, never both. Plan a small own test on current models, and compare the model rewrite with a code filter for numeric-only extraction.

source: Lin, Fu, Yang, Brahman, Huang, Bhagavatula, Ammanabrolu, Choi & Ren (2023) SwiftSage (NeurIPS 2023; arXiv 2305.17390); re-read for trigger set and missing ablations
finding: Switch from the fast module to the slow module when any of four conditions holds: 5 consecutive steps with zero reward; the predicted action is invalid; a critical decision (for example the final answer); an unexpected observation. After the slow module writes an action buffer the agent returns to the fast module when the buffer is empty; two consecutive invalid actions in the buffer send control back. Average score on 30 ScienceWorld task types: SwiftSage 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3. Tokens per action: SwiftSage 757.07 vs SayCan 1,855.84, ReAct 1,971.03, Reflexion 2,983.46. With GPT-3.5-turbo instead of GPT-4, ReAct fell from 36.43 to 19.76 and SwiftSage kept 62.22.
numbers: Fast-only ('Swift-Only') table with ChatGPT backend: short tasks 78.68 vs SwiftSage 72.81, medium 32.90 vs 55.34, long 35.55 vs 57.99. So on short tasks the fast module alone scored higher than the gated agent in that table.
limits: The paper has no ablation of the four triggers and no always-call-the-slow-module arm at equal tokens. All baselines call an LLM at every step. Only a text-simulator environment with a reward signal (the stuck rule needs reward). The authors list learning the switch as future work. I found no later study that copies the trigger set to a non-simulator task.
agent_relevance: For gap 8: the efficiency is real versus per-step LLM agents, but the claim that the trigger set beats always-deliberate at equal tokens is untested. A copy for our agent needs stand-ins, all codeable: no reward becomes no new verified evidence in N steps; invalid action becomes tool or format error; critical decision becomes before the final answer or an irreversible action; unexpected observation becomes a tool result that breaks a stated expectation.

source: Liang, Zhong, Yang & Quan (2025) ThinkSwitcher: when to think hard, when to think fast (arXiv 2505.14183)
finding: A small learned switch reads only the prompt and picks short or long chain-of-thought for the same model. Seven math benchmarks, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B. For the 7B model (average over seven benchmarks): short-only 46.0% at 1,079 tokens, long-only 64.6% at 7,617, ThinkSwitcher 62.8% at 5,405, random 25/75 mix 58.9% at 5,918, random 50/50 55.2% at 4,120, BERT classifier switch 60.7% at 6,021. So the switch kept about 90% of the long-versus-short gain ((62.8-46.0)/(64.6-46.0)) at about 71% of the long-mode tokens, and beat a random mix at similar tokens by about 4 points. The authors report 20 to 30% less compute for 1 to 2 points of accuracy. On the 1.5B model the BERT switch used fewer tokens but lost accuracy.
numbers: Thresholds chosen per model (0.04, 0.05, 0.03). Training signals come from the relative accuracy of the two modes on training questions.
limits: Math only, so no pattern, perception or distractor items (gap 2's mixed set is not tested). The switch is trained, not a hand-written structural rule. A BERT classifier on the prompt is the nearest thing to a cheap structural gate; it recovered less than the trained switch but was above a random mix at similar or slightly higher tokens for 7B and 14B. Distilled small reasoning models, not frontier models.
agent_relevance: For gap 2: a prompt-only gate can recover most of the best-mode gain on math at moderate token cost, and a cheap classifier beats a random mix. A hand rule (numbers, equals sign, multi-step) has not been measured against these, and nothing here covers the classes where step-by-step hurts (d15).

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi & Schwartz (2025) Don't overthink it: preferring shorter thinking chains for improved LLM reasoning (arXiv 2505.17813v2)
finding: Within one question, the shortest sampled chain beats a random one by up to 18.8 points and the longest by up to 34.5 points, and the shortest chains are 50% and 67% shorter than the random and longest. Method short-m@k: run k chains in parallel, stop when the first m finish thinking, majority vote among those m. Six reasoning LLMs including LN-Super-49B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B and R1-0528 (670B); benchmarks AIME 2024, AIME 2025, HMMT 2025 and GPQA-Diamond (198 questions). At matched total thinking tokens short-1@k beats majority@k at low budgets (up to about 45k, 60k and 100k total thinking tokens for R1-32B, QwQ-32B and R1-670B) and is beaten at larger budgets; for LN-Super-49B it beat majority across all budgets (57% accuracy at about 60% of the compute majority needs). short-3@k beat majority at all budgets (+2% at 80k tokens for QwQ-32B, about +4% at 100k for R1-670B). Fine-tuning on the shortest chains gave shorter outputs and better scores than fine-tuning on the longest.
numbers: Up to 40% fewer thinking tokens for short-1@k at equal accuracy; up to 33% wall-time reduction for short-3@k.
quote: shorter reasoning chains within individual questions are significantly more likely to yield correct answers
limits: Hard competition maths and science multiple choice; reasoning models; k parallel full-length attempts cut off early, which is not the same as a hard length cap or a short-prompted attempt. Not split by problem class. The authors say harder questions still need longer reasoning even though the shortest chain wins within a question.
agent_relevance: For gap 4: at equal total tokens, several parallel attempts with early stop and a selection rule beat waiting for everything on hard maths, at low to medium budgets. Whether capped short attempts beat one long attempt on our own task classes is still open; the evidence is only for reasoning models on maths and GPQA.

source: Gu, De, Markeeva, Velickovic & Pascanu (2026) Understanding performance gap between parallel and sequential sampling in large reasoning models (arXiv 2604.05868; Google DeepMind)
finding: Compared under the same NUMBER of solutions: independent parallel samples with majority vote outperform sequential refinement (each new attempt sees the earlier one) on AIME 2025 for Qwen3-14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B and Gemini 2.5 Flash, and also on coding. They tested three reasons: the aggregator, longer context in sequential runs, and less exploration because later samples condition on earlier answers. Aggregation and context length were not the main cause; lack of exploration was.
numbers: Models: Qwen3, R1-distilled, Gemini 2.5. Domains: competition maths and code. Exact accuracy gaps are in figures that I did not transcribe.
limits: Matches on number of solutions, not on total tokens, so it does not settle the token-equal question. Maths and code only.
agent_relevance: Indirect support for gap 4: a retry that sees its earlier wrong answer explores less. For our agent: make S6 retries independent (fresh context, no peek at the previous answer) when the aim is to escape a lure; use a sequential check only when the check brings an outside signal.

source: Kassenaar, Yang & Francois-Lavet (2026) Learning when to think: adaptive reasoning for test-time compute allocation (arXiv 2608.20256v2)
finding: A 1.5B distilled model picks NoThink, Short or Long as its first token, learned inside GRPO with per-mode caps (NoThink 1,024 tokens, Short 3,000, Long uncapped). On MATH500 (three seeds) accuracy was 0.782 vs base 0.796 while mean length fell from 4,796 to 2,811 tokens (41% less). The brief modes ended more accurate than Long, which the authors read as the router sorting by difficulty. On GSM8K it cut tokens 76% at higher accuracy than baselines at similar length, without retraining.
numbers: MATH500 held out; GSM8K transfer; three seeds.
limits: Small distilled model, reinforcement-learning training, maths only. Brief modes being more accurate than Long is confounded with difficulty because easy problems go to brief modes. Not a test at equal tokens against a fixed mix.
agent_relevance: Shows a three-way mode (none, short, long) is learnable and the cheap modes cover most easy items. Our scaffold has no training, so it can copy only the shape: three depths and a per-family record of which depth was enough.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (ICML 2025; arXiv 2410.21333v4); re-read for per-task numbers and the mapping
finding: Six tasks where verbal thinking hurts humans. Models were hurt on three: implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar; 4,400 problems from 100 grammars, 15 training strings each; GPT-4o 87.5% direct vs 64.4% CoT, -23.1; o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o direct 94.0% on a subset, -36.3; Claude 3 Opus 70.7 to 62.7), face recognition (500 problems; GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2, Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6, Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0 to 54.6; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 to 94.8), and classifying data with exceptions (rounds to learn the labels: GPT-4o 2.9 direct vs 12.5 CoT, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4; CoT stagnated near 80%, the share that are not exceptions). Not hurt: logical inconsistency (CoT HELPED: GPT-4o 53.2 to 93.9 on MNLI; humans were untrained in logic, models are not), spatial intuition (no significant change, for example GPT-4o 38 vs 40; models lack human motor simulation), working memory (CoT mostly helped, for example Claude 3.5 Sonnet 81 to 95 in the widest-gap range; models can hold all statements in context, humans cannot). Bootstrap against 378 zero-shot-vs-CoT comparisons from Sprague et al.: none of 100,000 resamples of 50 comparisons had a larger average drop than theirs.
numbers: See finding. Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3 and 3.1 (2024 era).
quote: In three of these tasks, state-of-the-art models exhibit significant performance drop-offs with CoT
limits: The authors say they do not expect the heuristic to predict perfectly. The three failures of the rule have a stated plausible pattern (model has trained logic that humans lack; model lacks sensorimotor priors; model has more memory capacity), but that pattern is post hoc: it was not predicted in advance and not tested on new tasks.
agent_relevance: For gap 10: our nearest task classes are the first and third (learning a rule from examples when there are exceptions, and noisy pattern or perceptual matching, as in grid puzzles): there more steps can hurt. A usable mapping rule: human harm from verbalising predicts model harm when the task is about statistical regularities or perception that words describe badly AND the model has the same limit; it fails when the model has a trained skill humans lack (logic) or a capacity humans lack (context). Treat it as a prior to check on our own pattern tasks, not a law.

source: Mukhopadhyay, Baral, Mahajan, Harish, RRV, Parmar, Nakamura & Baral (2025) Phantom Recall: when familiar puzzles fool smart models (arXiv 2510.11812)
finding: 25 well-known logic puzzles and 149 perturbations that keep the reasoning structure but change details or the answer. Eleven LLMs show near-perfect accuracy on the originals and clearly lower accuracy on the perturbed ones; the typical failure is to give the remembered solution (phantom recall) or to over-elaborate. Human-checked accuracy on the 149 perturbed puzzles: o3 59.73% (89/149), Gemini 2.5 Pro 58.39%, Claude Sonnet 4 54.36% (81/149), Gemini 2.5 Flash 48.32%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 46.31% (69/149), GPT-4o 29.53% (44/149). Thinking vs non-thinking within a family: GPT 59.73% vs 29.53%; Gemini 58.39% vs 48.32%; Claude 54.36% vs 46.31%. A prompt of explicit prohibitions ('do not use external knowledge', 'do not make assumptions') raised accuracy by 4.7 to 10.1 points on five open models (for example InternLM 26.8 to 36.9, Qwen 49.7 to 56.4) and about 10% on closed models.
numbers: Three human evaluators, average pairwise agreement 90.7%. The automated logical-equivalence judge agreed with humans on average 71%.
quote: while LLMs can remember reasoning, they often fail to re-reason
limits: Logic puzzles, not CRT arithmetic. Models are those of mid-2025, not the current ones. The mitigation is a constraint prompt, not a perturbation check or a rewrite of the problem, so S4 as designed was not tested.
agent_relevance: For gap 3: strong 2025 models still fail perturbed familiar items 40 to 50 percent of the time, even with thinking. With Ma 2025 (o1-preview 10.0% on principle-changed CRT) the lure still wins when the principle is changed. A perturbation check cannot be assumed to fix it; the constraint prompt helps modestly. No 2026 model was tested in any source I could open.

source: Malek, Ge, Lazic, Jin, Gyorgy & Szepesvari (2025) Frontier LLMs still struggle with simple reasoning tasks (Google DeepMind; arXiv 2507.07313)
finding: Unpuzzles: 97 famous puzzles with trivialised versions whose answer is obvious by common sense. Percent correct on puzzle vs unpuzzle: o3 87.6 vs 74.2; Gemini 2.5 Pro 93.8 vs 62.9; o1 86.7 vs 59.8; DeepSeek-R1 87.6 vs 59.8; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 77.3 vs 48.5; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 63.9 vs 27.8; GPT-4o 75.3 vs 19.6; Gemini 1.5 Pro 79.4 vs 17.5. The gap ranges from 9.1 points (o3) to 54 points. Thinking models do better than non-thinking ones, and newer models better than older. On a 64-item subset every model did better on context-shifted unpuzzles (same logic, new wording) than on the unpuzzles themselves, for example Gemini 2.5 Pro 66 vs 55, o1 59 vs 50, GPT-4o 52 vs 33; so the cause is similarity to the famous original. The paper also has procedurally generated easy tasks (counting, proof trees, travel planning) where even thinking models fail as length grows; o1 word counting falls below 40% at k>=3 and m>=2000.
numbers: Hand-graded by four annotators, one annotator per answer unless ambiguous. Models run in spring 2025. The text of the paper says 'better on the unpuzzles' where the table shows better on the puzzles; the table was used.
limits: Puzzles, not arithmetic traps. Small item count (97; 64 in the shifted subset). The gap shrinks with the model but does not vanish for the best model (o3).
agent_relevance: For gap 3: the lure effect on perturbed famous items shrinks with newer thinking models (gap 9.1 points for o3) but is still there. Rewording the problem away from the famous form (context shift) is what helped in their data, which supports S4's restate-in-new-surface-form step; they did not test that as an agent step.

source: Lei, Lin, Lu, Torr & Zou (2026) Thinking inertia: LLMs keep thinking when told not to (arXiv 2610.11765)
finding: Tests whether answer-directly instructions or thinking-off modes really give a no-thinking answer. Six LLMs (Qwen3 4B, 32B, 235B; DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B; GPT-5.4; Gemini-3-Flash), three question types (Boolean, multiple choice, open-ended), six prompt modes. Even with thinking mode off, DeepSeek-V4-Flash showed visible explicit inference in 99.9% of open-ended answers. Boolean tasks reach 80 to 100% answer-only compliance with thinking off; multiple choice ranges from near 0 to 95% across models. Strict answer-only prompting on open-ended tasks raised the answer-only rate from near zero to about 40% and cut mean accuracy by about 15 points across the five LLMs with thinking fully off.
numbers: The explicit-inference judge was GPT-5.5, checked against human annotation and a Claude Opus judge.
quote: visible explicit inference persists even under strict no-thinking controls
limits: Accuracy stays relatively stable on Boolean and multiple-choice; the 15-point loss is for open-ended tasks only.
agent_relevance: For gap 3 and S0: asking for a brief answer does not guarantee a first pass without reasoning. A test of whether the model falls for the trap when prompted for brief answers must log the visible pre-answer text, or the direct arm is partly a step-by-step arm. In our scaffold the fast route should be a short sampled answer with a hard token cap set in code, not a prompt request.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute (TMLR 12/2025; arXiv 2507.14417v2); re-read for setup
finding: Tasks where giving the model more reasoning budget lowers accuracy: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraint tracking, and advanced AI-risk probes. Five failure modes: Claude models become more distracted by irrelevant information; OpenAI o-series resist distractors but overfit to problem framing; models shift from sensible priors to spurious correlations; all models lose focus on complex deduction; longer reasoning may amplify some concerning behaviours (self-preservation in Claude Sonnet 4). Two setups: controlled (requested budget 0, 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, 8,192, 16,384 tokens, or low/medium/high for o-series) and natural (no explicit instruction). Actual token counts rise with the requested budget but not linearly.
numbers: Exact per-task accuracy curves are in figures; not transcribed here.
limits: Tasks were constructed because they show inverse scaling. It tests one long attempt at various lengths; it does not compare against several short attempts with the same total tokens. Models are mid-2025.
agent_relevance: For gap 4: supports capping length for distractor-heavy and constraint-tracking classes. Nothing here compares one long attempt with 3 to 4 short ones at equal total tokens, so gap 4 stays open; the nearest equal-token comparison is Hassid (d12), on maths and GPQA.

source: Ma, Xie, Wang, Sun, Chen, Wang, Liu & Tong (2025) Do large language models truly grasp mathematics? An empirical exploration from cognitive psychology (arXiv 2410.14979v6); re-read for o1 numbers
finding: Experiment II changes the mathematical principle of CRT1, CRT2 and CRT3 items while keeping the wording close (additive to non-additive cost; worker-count-dependent to independent; exponential to linear growth). Accuracy collapses: on modified CRT3 items 71.5% to 85.7% of the five models' answers treated the problem as exponential growth; for CRT1, 95.9% of errors applied the original method; for CRT2, 52.8% did. In Experiment III o1-preview kept its accuracy when only numbers changed but averaged 10.0% on principle-changed items; 82.5% of its wrong answers reused the original solution. Other cases: Claude 3 fell from 62.0% to 22.0% on modified CRT2 (chi-square(1)=14.82, p<.001); another model fell from 65.3% to 28.0%. Experiment I (numbers only): average accuracy 86.8% on type A and 68.5% on type B items.
numbers: Five LLMs plus o1-preview; 50 CRT3 problems from Hagendorff; five researchers as the human comparison, each answering 20% of the items. Number-only changes did not hurt o1.
limits: Small human group and a lab-built item set; modified items were checked by a second researcher. Models are late-2024 (Claude 3, GPT-4, Gemini 1.5, GLM-4, o1-preview). The paper does not test whether a perturbation check helps. Same paper as c17; the o1 numbers were re-read here.
agent_relevance: For gap 3: the pattern is lure reuse (82.5% of o1's wrong answers), and it appears only when the principle changes, not the numbers. So an S4 perturbation must change the principle, not just the numbers, or it will pass the trap. No source tested a perturbation step on a current model.
